American inventor and businessman, holder of 1,093 U.S. patents. Edison is known for his work on the [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent light bulb]], the [[Phonograph|phonograph]], [[Electric power distribution|electric power distribution]], and early motion pictures. Born in Milan, Ohio, he grew up in Port Huron, [[Michigan]], the seventh and last child of Samuel Ogden Edison Jr. and Nancy Matthews Elliott. He attended school for only a few months, learning from his mother, a former school teacher, and from reading on his own. His hearing declined from age 12, and he later believed the loss helped him concentrate. At 13 he sold newspapers, candy, and vegetables on trains and founded the *Grand Trunk Herald*. From 1863 to 1869 he held night-shift [[Telegraphy|telegraphy]] jobs in several states, and by 22 he had sold a few early inventions and moved to New York City. By 29 he owned a telegraph recorder factory in Newark with over one hundred employees.

His Menlo Park laboratory, established in 1876, is considered the first industrial research laboratory, and the phonograph made him internationally famous. In 1878 he began work on an electrical lighting system meant to replace gas lamps. In the "War of the Currents," he championed [[Direct current|direct current]] and was criticized for publicizing the dangers of alternating current through animal electrocutions aimed at rivals such as [[George Westinghouse]]. Competition from Westinghouse's system forced him to yield, and the merger of the Edison General Electric Company with Thomson-Houston produced [[General Electric]]. Later he founded a cement company, built a motion picture camera, and ran firms making batteries, films, records, and phenol. His last project was a search for domestic rubber production. He had troubled relationships with his children, and he lived with diabetes.

Cognitive process in which the [[Mind|mind]] considers, creates, or manipulates ideas, representations, or information. Core forms include judging, reasoning, concept formation, problem solving, and deliberation. Memory and imagination are also frequently counted as types of thought. Thought may arise in response to [[Perception|perception]] but can also occur without immediate sensory input. In a broad sense, any mental event, including unconscious processes, may be called thought, and the term can also denote the resulting mental states or systems of ideas.

Theories of thinking differ. Platonism holds that thought discerns eternal forms and their interrelations, distinguishing them from imperfect sensory imitations. Aristotelianism interprets it as instantiating the universal essence of an object within the mind, derived from sense experience. Inner speech theories describe thought as silent verbal expression, in a natural language or in a "mental language," or Mentalese, as proposed by the language of thought hypothesis. Associationism views it as a succession of ideas governed by laws of association, while [[Behaviorism|behaviorism]] reduces it to behavioral dispositions. Computationalism compares it to information processing in computers. These theories are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

Recognized types include judgement, which affirms or denies a proposition; reasoning, which draws conclusions from premises or evidence; problem solving, which aims at specific goals; and deliberation, which weighs possible courses of action. Thinking is often contrasted with feeling, seen as rational and dispassionate. Many disciplines study thought. [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|Phenomenology]] examines its subjective experience, [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychology]] treats it as information processing, and [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalysis]] stresses unconscious processes. Neuroscience, linguistics, and artificial intelligence also investigate it. The word derives from Old English *þoht*.

Geometric model in which three values, called coordinates, are required to determine the position of a point. Most commonly the term means three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], which models physical space; more general three-dimensional spaces are called 3-manifolds. In classical physics it serves as a model of the universe in which all known matter exists, and in [[General relativity|relativity theory]] it is a local subspace of space-time. Any three directions not lying in one plane may serve as coordinate directions; when pairwise perpendicular, the values are often labeled width, height or depth, and length.

In the [[Cartesian coordinate system]], three axes, usually labeled x, y, and z, are perpendicular to one another at the origin, and each point is given by an ordered triple of real numbers measuring its distance from the planes determined by the other two axes. Cylindrical and spherical coordinates are other common methods. The set of such triples is denoted ℝ³.

[[Aristotle]] held that three dimensions are all there are, since what is divisible in three directions is divisible in all. Books XI to XIII of [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's *Elements*]] treat solid geometry, including perpendicularity, parallelism, and the five regular Platonic solids. In the 17th century [[René Descartes]] described space with coordinates in *La Géométrie*, and Pierre de Fermat independently developed similar ideas. In the 18th century [[Leonhard Euler]] derived the first analytical geodesic equation and, with Gaspard Monge, laid foundations for differential geometry. In the 19th century [[William Rowan Hamilton]] developed quaternions and coined the terms scalar and vector. Josiah Willard Gibbs later identified the dot and cross products in their own right, and Arthur Cayley applied matrix mathematics to n-dimensional geometry.

Continuous progression of existence in an apparently irreversible succession from the past, through the present, and into the future. Time sequences events, compares their durations or the intervals between them, and quantifies rates of change in material reality or conscious experience. It is often called the fourth dimension, in addition to the three spatial dimensions. Time has been a central subject of study in religion, philosophy, and science, and temporal measurement has been a prime motivation in navigation and astronomy.

Defining time without circularity has eluded scholars. Traditional definitions relied on periodic motion such as the sun's apparent path, the phases of the moon, and the swing of a pendulum. In physics, time is a fundamental concept used to define quantities such as velocity and is operationally defined as "what a clock reads," a count of repeating events such as the SI second. Physicists developed the concept of [[Spacetime|spacetime]], in which events have four coordinates, three for space and one for time. Under [[General relativity|general relativity]] time can be dilated by velocity and matter, though the effect is negligible outside extreme conditions such as relativistic speeds or the gravity of black holes. Measurable time is believed to have begun with the [[Big Bang]] 13.8 billion years ago. Reconciling general relativity with quantum mechanics, in which time is a universal and absolute parameter, is called the problem of time, and no generally accepted theory of quantum general relativity exists.

Measurement takes two forms: the [[Calendar|calendar]], used for periods longer than a day, and the clock, used for shorter periods. The [[Second|second]], the SI base unit, is defined by the electronic transition frequency of caesium atoms. Artifacts from the Paleolithic suggest the moon was used to reckon time at least 6,000 years ago. Lunar calendars had years of 12 or 13 lunar months (354 or 384 days), and lunisolar calendars add a thirteenth month to some years. The Maya developed interrelated calendars, including a 260-day sacred calendar, the Tzolk'in. The reforms of [[Julius Caesar]] in 45 BC put the Roman world on a solar calendar, which Pope Gregory XIII corrected in 1582; the [[Gregorian calendar]] is now the most commonly used worldwide. The French Republican Calendar, with ten hours of a hundred minutes of a hundred seconds in each day, was abolished in 1806. Egyptians are credited with dividing the day into smaller parts using the [[Sundial|sundial]]; obelisks used as gnomons were built as early as c. 3500 BC, and a device dating to c. 1500 BC also measured time by shadow.

Turco-Mongol conqueror, first ruler of the Timurid dynasty and founder of the [[Timurid Empire]], which ruled over modern-day Afghanistan, Iran, and Central Asia. Also known as Tamerlane, Timur was born into the Turkicized Mongol confederation of the Barlas in Transoxiana. By 1370 he controlled the western Chagatai Khanate, and from there led campaigns that defeated the Khans of the [[Golden Horde]], the [[Mamluk Sultanate]] in Egypt and Syria, the emerging [[Ottoman Empire]], and the [[Delhi Sultanate]] in the Indian subcontinent. He made [[Samarkand]] his capital.

His origins are debated. Historian Peter Jackson considers it generally accepted that Timur was of "unimpeachable Mongol ancestry," and Timurid histories trace his paternal descent to a male-line ancestor of [[Genghis Khan]]. No written evidence from Timur's lifetime or earlier, however, makes such a link to him directly. He sought to revive Genghis Khan's legacy and saw himself as restorer of the Mongol Empire, and by the end of his reign he controlled the remnants of the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate, and the Golden Horde and had even attempted to restore the Yuan dynasty in China.

Timur's armies were multi-ethnic and much feared, and his campaigns laid waste to large parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. Scholars estimate that they caused the deaths of millions of people. He also patronized scholars and poets such as Ibn Khaldun and Hafez, and his reign led to the Timurid Renaissance. He died while on the way to invade Ming China, and his empire fragmented shortly afterward. He was the grandfather of [[Ulugh Beg]], an astronomer and mathematician who ruled Central Asia from 1411 to 1449, and the great-great-great-grandfather of Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire.

Capital and most populous city of [[Japan]] (pop., 2023: over 14 million), at the head of Tokyo Bay on the central coast of [[Honshu]]. Officially the Tokyo Metropolis, it is Japan's economic center and the seat of its government and emperor. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025. Its central 23 special wards, including Chiyoda, Shinjuku, and Shibuya, formerly made up Tokyo City; since 1943 its governing structure has resembled that of a prefecture.

Originally called Edo, the city rose to prominence in 1603 as the seat of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]]. By the mid-18th century it had grown from a small fishing village into one of the world's largest cities, with over one million people. After the [[Meiji Restoration]] (1868), the imperial capital was moved there from [[Kyoto]] and the city was renamed Tokyo, meaning "Eastern Capital." It was greatly damaged by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and by Allied bombing in [[World War II]]. Rapid reconstruction beginning in the late 1940s fueled the Japanese economic miracle.

Tokyo was the first Asian city to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics, in 1964, and hosted them again in 2021. Its gross domestic output was 120.2 trillion yen (US$887.9 billion) in fiscal year 2022, 21.2% of Japan's total. It remains a leading financial hub, and the Tokyo Stock Exchange is among the world's top five. The [[University of Tokyo]] is Japan's top-ranking university. Tokyo Station is the central hub of the [[Shinkansen]] high-speed railway, and Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest train station.

Object that extends an individual's ability to modify the surroundings or accomplish a task, typically solid, hand-operated, non-biological, and of a single broad purpose, unlike machines or computers. Humans make and use tools more than any other animal, including using tools to make other tools, but many animals also use tools. In 1981 Benjamin Beck published a widely used definition of tool use, later modified: the external employment of an unattached or manipulable attached object to alter the form, position, or condition of another object, another organism, or the user, with the user holding and directly manipulating it. By extension, concepts that support systematic thought are often called "tools" or "toolkits."

Anthropologists regard tool use as an important step in human evolution. Because humans and wild [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzees]] both use tools extensively, the first routine use is widely assumed to predate their divergence, though early tools were probably perishable, such as sticks. Stone artifacts date back about 2.5 million years, but a 2010 study suggests that *Australopithecus afarensis* carved animal carcasses with stone implements about 3.4 million years ago. Actual tools at least 2.6 million years old have been found in Ethiopia, and the hand axe is one of the earliest distinguishable forms. Early tools of stone, bone, and wood served for food preparation, hunting, weapons, clothing, pottery, and construction. The development of [[Metalworking|metalworking]] made new types possible, and harnessing animal power, wind, or steam allowed increasingly complex tools.

Several of the six classic [[Simple machine|simple machines]] (wheel and axle, lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and screw) were invented in [[Mesopotamia]]. The wheel and axle first appeared with the potter's wheel in the 5th millennium BC, the lever in the shadoof c. 3000 BC, pulleys in the early 2nd millennium BC, and the screw in the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BC). Water wheels and watermills date to before 350 BC. Use of mechanical devices expanded in ancient Greece and Rome through waterwheels, and later windmills. Machine tools, with origins among 18th-century clock, watch, and instrument makers, surged during the [[Industrial Revolution]] and enabled precise, economical [[Interchangeable parts|interchangeable parts]]. Widespread [[Automation|automation]] in the 19th and 20th centuries let tools operate with minimal human supervision.

Branch of mathematics concerned with the properties of a geometric object that are preserved under continuous deformations such as stretching, twisting, crumpling, and bending, but not closing or opening holes, tearing, or gluing.

A [[Topological space]] is a set with a structure, called a topology, that allows continuous deformation to be defined. Examples include Euclidean spaces and, more generally, [[Metric space|metric spaces]], since any metric defines a topology. The deformations considered are homeomorphisms and homotopies, and a property invariant under them is a topological property. Basic examples are dimension, which distinguishes a line from a surface; compactness, which distinguishes a line from a circle; and connectedness, which distinguishes a circle from two non-intersecting circles. Intuitively, two spaces are homeomorphic if one can be deformed into the other without cutting or gluing, so a topologist cannot distinguish a coffee mug from a doughnut.

The underlying ideas go back to [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], who in the 17th century envisioned *geometria situs* and *analysis situs*. [[Leonhard Euler]]'s 1736 paper on the [[Seven Bridges of Königsberg]] showed that no route through the town (now Kaliningrad) could cross each bridge exactly once, a result depending only on connectivity, and the problem led to [[Graph theory|graph theory]]. His polyhedron formula, V − E + F = 2, is regarded by some authorities as the first theorem of topology. Johann Benedict Listing introduced the term *Topologie* in 1847, and the English form appeared in 1883 in his obituary in *Nature*. [[Henri Poincaré]] consolidated and extended their work, and his 1895 paper *Analysis Situs* introduced the concepts now known as [[Homotopy|homotopy]] and homology. The idea of a topological space was developed only in the first decades of the 20th century.

[[Travel]] for pleasure, and the commercial activity of providing and supporting such travel. UN Tourism defines it more generally as people "staying in places outside their usual environment for not more than one consecutive year for leisure and not less than 24 hours, business and other purposes." The English words *tourist* (1772) and *tourism* (1811) derive from *tour*, from Old French *torner*, from Latin *tornare*, "to turn on a lathe."

Definitions have shifted over time. In 1936 the [[League of Nations]] defined a foreign tourist as someone traveling abroad for at least 24 hours, and the [[United Nations]] amended this in 1945 to include a maximum stay of six months. In 1994 the UN identified three forms: domestic tourism, by residents within their own country; inbound tourism, by non-residents entering a country; and outbound tourism, by residents traveling to another country. The terms tourism and tourist are sometimes used pejoratively to imply a shallow interest in the places visited, whereas traveler is often a mark of distinction.

International tourism receipts grew to US$1.03 trillion in 2005, and international tourist arrivals passed 1 billion for the first time in 2012. Numbers declined between the second half of 2008 and the end of 2009 because of the [[Great Recession]] and the 2009 H1N1 influenza outbreak, then recovered until the [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID-19 pandemic]] ended the growth. The World Tourism Organization estimated that international arrivals might have fallen by 58% to 78% in 2020, a potential loss of US$0.9–1.2 trillion in receipts. Global tourism accounts for approximately 8% of greenhouse-gas emissions, and many organizations are shifting toward [[Sustainability|sustainable]] tourism to balance economic benefits with environmental and social responsibility.

Type of [[Human settlement|human settlement]], generally larger than a [[Village|village]] but smaller than a [[City|city]]. Criteria for distinguishing a town vary globally and may depend on population size, economic character, administrative status, or historical significance. In some regions towns are defined by legal charters or government designations, while elsewhere the term is informal. Towns typically have centralized services, infrastructure, and governance, and serve as hubs for commerce, education, and culture.

Usage differs by country. In the U.K. a town may derive its status from a market-town designation or royal charter, and is typically served by a town council. In the U.S. the term is often applied to incorporated municipalities, which have legally defined borders and local government; an unincorporated town lacks its own governance. In Australia and Canada, distinctions between towns, cities, and rural areas rest on population thresholds. The UN-endorsed Degree of Urbanization framework treats a town as a contiguous area of at least 5,000 inhabitants with a density of 300 or more people per sq km. Population alone is an unreliable guide: in India a large village may hold several times the population of a small town, and some U.K. historical cities are far smaller than its larger towns. Today's towns usually differ from villages and hamlets in that most residents earn a living from manufacturing, commerce, and public services rather than agriculture.

The word shares an origin with German *Zaun* ("fence"), Dutch *tuin* ("garden, yard; fence, enclosure"), and Old Norse *tún* ("enclosure, as for a homestead"). The original sense in Germanic and Celtic was a fortress or enclosure. Old English *tūn* became a common place-name suffix in England and southeastern Scotland.
